title: Cicoria Ripassata
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Boiled chicory greens quickly re-sautéed in garlic and chili-infused olive oil, a beloved simple side dish that pairs the vegetable's earthy bitterness with just enough richness.
longDesc: The technique of boiling greens first and then 'passing' them a second time through hot oil and garlic (ripassare, literally 'to pass again') is a defining method across Italian home cooking, applied here to Rome's beloved chicory.
ingredients: 1 kg (2.2 lb) chicory or dandelion greens, trimmed
80 ml (⅓ cup) extra virgin olive oil
steps: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil and cook the chicory for 8-10 minutes until tender.
Drain well, pressing out excess water.
Warm the olive oil in a large pan and sauté the garlic and chilies until fragrant, taking care not to burn the garlic.
Add the drained chicory and toss to coat, cooking for 5 minutes until well combined and lightly crisped at the edges.
Season with salt and serve hot.
chefTips: Pressing out excess water from the boiled greens before the second sauté helps them crisp slightly rather than steam.
A generous hand with garlic and chili is traditional and helps balance the greens' natural bitterness.
This technique works well with many bitter greens beyond chicory, including cime di rapa or dandelion greens.
commonMistakes: Not draining the boiled greens well enough, resulting in a watery rather than lightly crisped final dish.
Burning the garlic in the hot oil, which turns bitter.
Overcooking the greens in the initial boil, losing their texture entirely.
reheating: Reheat gently in a pan with a little olive oil.
healthBenefits: Chicory is rich in fiber and has traditionally been valued for its digestive properties.
culturalNote: Cicoria ripassata is a staple side dish throughout Lazio and much of central and southern Italy, the boil-then-sauté technique a fundamental method in Italian vegetable cookery.
